features.name: The selva oscura — the trackless wood
features.note: Rebuilt 2026-09-08 and verified on the running page. 200 x 195 m, ~190 canopy trees of 24-36 m with the crown base at 10-17 m, 560 thickets and 1 200 bramble cards under them. Species corrected to the 1499 (ll. 555-563): oak, holm oak, ash, elm-with-vine, and NO beech and NO fir. The path corridor is gone.

features.name: The hungry wolf that watches the path
features.note: Moved 2026-09-08 to (-21, 132), on the gravel plain of the SECOND dream and on the left hand (-x under the declared compass), per Dall. p. 23. It was at (4.2, 40.5) in the dark wood beside the path.

features.name: Poliphilo's prayer to Jupiter, which delivers him
features.note: The dream mode narrates it; nothing in the world marks the place.

features.name: The spacious plain the dream opens on
features.source: 1499 l. 530-540 ("una spatiosa planitie, tutta virente et di multiplici fiori"); Dallington p. 14
features.note: The ground is there beyond the wood (z 413-483) but nothing is staged on it. The book's plain is defined by ABSENCE -- no man, no beast, no bird, no house, no flock -- and absence still has to be composed: flowers, a level horizon, and the silence.

features.name: The wood roofed like a vault, so the sun does not reach the ground
features.source: 1499 ll. 555-563 ("come da camurato culmo di densante fronde coperto, non penetrava l'alma luce"); Dallington pp. 14-17
features.note: Verified: the floor is in shadow and the sky is shut overhead. Built as four opaque leaf-mass shells a tree at r = 0.42 h, interlocking at 14 m spacing, plus twenty large sprays. The floor is separately dark in albedo because the hemisphere, ambient and environment light are not occluded by geometry and shadow alone cannot do it. Prerequisite delivered the same day: the sun's shadow box now follows the walker (HPStyles.trackedSun).

features.name: The trackless wood, and the sun kept on one side
features.source: Dallington p. 15 ("could not finde any track or path"; "the keeping of the sunne still vpon one side, to direct mee streight forwarde")
features.note: The 5.4 m corridor is gone and the five clearings are in, so the sun's bearing can be recovered from the shafts and the book's "keeping of the sunne still vpon one side" works. What is missing: nothing tells the player that is the way out. Poliphilo's own layer or the station note should say it.

features.name: The broad mighty oak in a spacious green mead
features.note: A 31 m oak at (9, 193) in an open mead with five outliers, a long way from the river because he lost the water chasing the song.

research.enumerated_by: read end to end against Dallington 1592, session of 2026-09-09
research.note: Read from the chapter's own argument (the horse, the elephant, and the porch) through the forecourt, the colonnades, the horse and his base, the colossus inside and out, the woman's head, and the elephant's obelisk. The 2026-09-08 pass had read this chapter for measurements only and left 4 features; this pass adds 12. The largest finds are the porch's own thirty-pace forecourt and its two areostyle colonnades, which are a whole architectural setting the world does not have, and the loop-holes that light the colossus within -- which the interior opened the same day needs and has not got.

features.name: The pyramid-portal at the size the book gives it
features.source: Dallington pp. 26-31; 1499 l. 905; Bury 1998 Appendix (Word & Image 14.1-2, corpus md ll. 845-890)
features.note: Base 6 stadia + 20 paces = 1 139.6 m wide; base storey 37 m; plinth 1 110 m wide and 20.7 m high; pyramid 1 110 m square and about 785 m tall by Colonna's own construction (edge = base side), 1 410 courses of 0.56 m; cube 5.9 m; obelisk 10.4 m. Total to the nymph about 865 m. Built today at 17.5 m wide and 21 m tall. Bury: the huge figures are deliberate, "to sustain the romantic fiction that the ruin discovered by Poliphilus surpassed all the wonders of the ancient world". Full table in DIMENSIONS.md 2.

features.name: The valley walls the pyramid stops dead
features.source: Dallington p. 27 ("the foresaid valley there had an end, that no man could go further forward or backe againe, but to enter in by this broade, large, and wide open porche"); p. 31 (10 paces of clearance to the cliff each side)
features.note: Two ridges converging from a 150 m gap to 40 m at the piers, with ashlar curtain walls carrying the building out to the rock on both sides and wall colliders behind them. Dall. p. 27's "no man could go further forward or backe againe" is now true: the porch is the only way through. The cliffs' lower slopes carry the fir, pine and cypress that belong to a mountain.

features.name: The recumbent colossus, sixty paces long
features.source: Dallington p. 44 ("his length was three score paces")
features.note: 88.8 m from head to foot, climbed by the beard to the breast and entered through the mouth and down the throat. Built, but at roughly a tenth of that, so the climb-in that the text describes does not read.

features.name: The Medusa door and the descending stair, both on the right hand
features.note: The Gorgon head is carved in the plinth "vpon the right hand as I went"; the stair down opens "vpon my right hand against one of the collaterall and side-lying mountaines". Nobody has checked which side the world puts them on. Under the compass frame proposed in DIRECTIONS.md 2 the right hand is east (+x).

features.name: The four-square court before the porch, thirty paces across
features.note: A court of thirty paces by its diameter, paved in fine marble and worked chequerwise in several colours -- and broken and overgrown in many places by the ruin of the old walk and its pillars. The world has chequered pavements at the palace and in the bath, but nothing identified as the porch's own forecourt. Needs a look on the running page before this is called unbuilt.

features.name: Two areostyle colonnades, right and left toward the mountains
features.note: Two straight rows of pillars running from the front of the porch toward the mountains on either hand, set areostyle with fifteen paces between pillar and pillar. Capitals of waved shell-work and drapery, the corners turned in like a curled lock of hair, and the capital three times the width of the column's foot. Most stand; many are widowed of their capitals, with astragals, shafts and bases buried in the ruin. Poliphilo guesses it was a riding-ring or a covered walk. Grepped for areostyle and for a colonnade at the porch: nothing.

features.name: Plane trees, wild olives, pine and brambles at the colonnade's foot
features.note: Old plane trees, wild olives, pine and pricking brambles growing hard against the rows of pillars. The detail that makes the colonnade a RUIN rather than a building: what has taken it is scrub, not weather.

features.name: The winged vaulting horse, and the youths thrown from him
features.note: Moulten brass, wings fanning out, standing on a smooth base five feet broad and nine long. Head free and unbridled; two small ears, one forward and one drawn back; a long waved mane falling from the crest on the contrary side. Youths try to ride and not one keeps his seat: some thrown flat, some grovelling, some headlong between the horse and the earth, some holding vainly by the mane, some climbing on, some struggling out from under his feet. Built as _buildColossalHorse; the RIDERS are what to check -- the passage is mostly about them, and the world may have the horse without them.

features.name: The two dances on the base: TEMPVS and AMISSIO
features.note: Built (world/portal.js, the TEMPVS AMISSIO horse, with Buffalo Hand E's note). Two companies in semicircles with a partition between, one inscribed TEMPVS; on the contrary side youths gathering flowers while nymphs snatch them away, inscribed AMISSIO.

features.name: The loop-holes and wickets that light the colossus within
features.note:
Built and seen on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=364, standing inside the passage at (40.5, 4): two pierced openings show in the vault crown overhead, warm light falls across the belly vault ahead, and the organ plaques are readable where before the passage was a dark tube.

Six wickets pierced through the crown of the vaults, set alternately off the axis so the light rakes across the organ doors on the south wall instead of pooling down the middle. Their heights follow the vaults they pierce -- the chest's crown is 3.88 m inside and the belly's 2.79, off the vault radii -- so each sits a little under. Every other one carries a point light; six inside one figure would cost more than the light is worth, and the shafts read from the emissive alone.

Found by reading chapter III end to end, hours after the interior was opened. The book had the fixture the new interior needed, which is the argument for reading a chapter whole rather than for the thing you happen to be building. Cost: +2 meshes, +12 triangles.

features.name: Every part named in three tongues, with its disease, cause and cure
features.note: Each part of the body carries its own name in Chaldee, Greek and Latin -- entrails, sinews, bones, veins, muscles and flesh -- with the disease bred there, its cause, and its cure and remedy. The world labels six organs in Latin with an English gloss, so the THREE TONGUES are not there, and neither is the cause/cure structure. Note the tension to resolve: Dallington says the cures ARE written here, while the heart's are the ones Poliphilo does not divulge.

features.name: The climb in: by the beard to the breast, and down the throat
features.note: You mount by the hairs of his beard to the breast, and by the torn pieces of it to the mouth, which stays open and empty; then down by degrees into the throat, to the stomach, and by secret ways to all the inward parts. Since 2026-09-09 the figure IS entered through the mouth and walked down the body -- but on the level, at ground height. The book's entry is a CLIMB, and the descent by degrees into the throat is a stair.

features.name: The groaning: air through the mouth and the pipes of the throat
features.note: Air getting in and coming forth of the wide mouth and the hollow pipes of the throat makes a moderated, timed groaning like a sick man near death -- it is what draws Poliphilo to the figure at all, and he says his hair stood up. Declined as SOUND: the site is silent by design (DECISIONS.md 2026-09-04). Worth reopening as a visible or written cue, since without it nothing explains why he climbs in.

features.name: His sigh makes the whole brazen colossus resound
features.note: At the heart he reads how love begets sorrow, calls out upon Polia, and the whole colossus of brass resounds and strikes him into a horrible fear. Declined as sound, per the same 2026-09-04 call. The echo at the horse (p. 37) is already carried as an utterance rather than as audio, which is the pattern to follow.

features.name: The woman's head, of like bigness, buried in the fallen stones
features.note: On the other side, of like bigness to the first, the upper part of a woman's head part bare and the rest buried in decayed ruin -- and heaps of disordered fallen stone FORBID him to view it, so he turns away. The world builds her as a half-buried figure with vaults; the book shows only the crown of a head and a refusal of access. The refusal is the point (Priki).

features.name: His sigh returns as an echo in the solitary place
features.note: His breathing, in the thick air of that solitary place, gives an echo and puts him in mind of Polia. Carried in the world as the horse station's attitude (constants.js: horse -> listening, his own sigh comes back off the stone).

research.note: Had ZERO features and its own block said nobody had enumerated it. Read from the naming of the four wonders through the proportion figure, the digression on the architect, the right-hand stylobate and the forge relief cut on it, to the point where he goes in at the porch. Adds 8. Three of them are the chapter's plates, left at `unknown` rather than `unbuilt` because they have not been read against the world yet, which is the recipe's rule. The largest find is that this chapter is mostly ARCHITECTURAL THEORY -- the porch is the occasion for the book to state its own rule of proportion and its own picture of the architect -- and the world carries none of it.

features.name: The four wonders named as one set: porch, horse, colossus, elephant
features.note: Poliphilo is given leave to consider 'these foure rare wonders' and names them together: the porch or gate, the horse, the colossus, the elephant. All four are built. What is wrong is that they are not one set on the ground: the horse, colossus and elephant stand past the portal while the book has them in the court before it. See ticket bug-piazza-wrong-side-of-portal, which this line is the clearest evidence for -- the four are a single company in a single place.

features.name: The construction of the porch's proportion, drawn on the ground
features.note: Poliphilo works out the architect's rule by drawing it: he takes a square off the two columns either side, makes a tetragon ABCD, divides it with three lines each way into sixteen quadrats, adds half as much again to get twenty-four, draws the two diagonals and two more lines to make four quadrats mutually intersecting, then sets four median points in the void over the isopleures and joins them into a rhombus. This is the book being a treatise for a page, and it is the reason the porch is described at all. Nothing in the world shows it; grepping for tetragon, rhombus and quadrat finds only unrelated canvas code.

features.name: What the architect must be, and the rule of the solid
features.note: The digression the proportion figure sets off. Take away order and rule and nothing can be made beautiful or durable; ornament may be added or diminished, but the SOLID -- the body of the frame, its invention and symmetry -- must be kept whole. Then the architect himself: honest, no prattler, courteous, patient, full of new devices, a curious searcher into all arts, and not subject to avarice. Belongs in the commentary layer rather than in geometry, but it is one of the few places the book states its own method, and the world does not carry it anywhere.

features.name: The right-hand stylobate, an altar-like pedestal of white alabaster
features.note:
Below on the right hand, a square stone like an altar set under the bases of the columns, with a fitting cornice above and the same below, wrought about its sides with leaves and hollowed under with a gulaterie, the leaf-work hemming in a smooth face of shining white alabaster, polished and plain. It is the ground the relief below is cut on. Not built: portal.js knows the word stylobate only in a comment listing the terms of chapters XVII-XXXVIII.

BUILT and seen on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=367: cornice below, an alabaster body 1.5 m square, cornice above, leaf-work hemming the face and the gulaterie hollowed under, standing against the porch's eastern jamb at (7.6, 27.9) so its carved face looks back up the approach. The right hand is derived, not assumed: he faces the porch from the north, so faces -z, and (0,0,-1) x (0,1,0) = (1,0,0) -- right is +x.

features.name: The forge of Vulcan on the pedestal: Venus, Cupid and Mars
features.note:
The relief cut on that alabaster face, and the most fully described picture in the chapter. A middle-aged smith of churlish countenance with an unshapely beard, in a goatskin apron knotted behind, sitting at an anvil fixed on a knotty stump, hammer raised over a brigandine of burning metal. Before him a winged goddess holding her naked infant on her thighs, her foot set on a stone by a furnace sunk in a hollow, her hair dressed high -- and the smiths at their work cannot stop looking at her. Beside them a knight in brass armour with the head of Medusa on the breastplate, a baldric across his chest, a half-pike raised and a high-crested helmet; and behind the smith a young man in silk, seen only from the breast up over the smith's bowed head. Venus, Cupid, Mars and Vulcan: the quarrel the whole book is about, cut on the gate you enter by.

BUILT 2026-09-09 and seen on the running page at main.js?v=368. It was PARTIAL for one tick: the panel was cut and named but the carving came from the shared _reliefTexture, which seeds a generic crowd off the scene name, so five identical figures stood in for the most fully described picture in chapters III-IV.

_reliefTexture now dispatches to a named scene first and falls back to the seeded crowd only where the book merely gestures at a relief. The forge is drawn figure by figure: the young man in silk behind, seen from the breast up over the smith's bowed head; the smith with his beard turning into his chin, in the goatskin apron hung between his legs, seated on his stone with the hammer up; the anvil on its knotty stump with the brigandine on it; the winged goddess with her hair dressed high and the infant on her thighs, her foot on a stone; the furnace sunk in its hollow with the fire in it; and the knight with the high crest, the Medusa on the breastplate, the baldric and the half-pike raised.

The register is carved silhouette -- each shape drawn twice, dark below and light above, which is how every relief in this world is made. It is not fine drawing and does not try to be. Cost: nothing. Identical mesh and triangle counts either side, because it is a texture.

features.name: The ancient gate with medallion busts
features.note: Attached to this chapter in the plate index. Grepping portal.js for medallion returns nothing, so the busts are probably absent, but the plate has not been read against the built gate and this is marked unknown rather than unbuilt on purpose -- the recipe's rule.

features.note: Attached to this chapter in the plate index and not yet read against the world. The world builds hieroglyphs elsewhere (_hiero, the ant and the elephant), so the vocabulary exists; whether THIS set is among them is unchecked.

The eight-sided bath, ΑΣΑΜΙΝΘΟΣ
features.note: Rebuilt 2026-09-06 to the text: jacinth columns, black tables in coral jasper, ivory nymphs, the zophor of boys and sea-monsters, oak-leaf ribs, the lion-head censer, the fish mosaic.

features.name: The fruitful fields: the worked countryside
features.source: Dallington p. 90 ("a fayre and plentifull countrie, fruitefull fieldes, and fertile groundes")
features.note: Built 2026-09-07. Hunt reads the book through the three natures and the world had the first (the selva oscura) and the third (the courts) and nothing between them. Strip fields with real ridge-and-furrow, an orchard of apple/pear/plum in quincunx, and the arbustum -- vines married to elms, ch. I l. 625. Station key `fields`.

features.name: The ancient bridge, and the spring that divides right and left
features.note: "scaturiva una larga vena di chiarissima aqua viva, la quale dividentese faceva dui correnti fluenticuli, uno alla dextra et alla sinistra l'altro" — banks of stone and shade with the straddling roots laid bare, hung with maidenhair fern and cymbalaria. A legible piece of geography the fields station lacks.

features.name: The wooded district ringed by a tree-bearing mountain, conifers on its slopes
features.note: "silvosa contrata circunclusa dall'arborifera montagna": black and white poplars, riverside alder, manna-ash and flowering oleander on the water; tall single-stemmed fir, weeping larch and silver fir on the mountains. This is where the conifers belong — putting fir in the dark wood took them from the wrong passage entirely. See WOODS.md 3.

features.name: The octagonal fountain-house first glimpsed through the trees
features.source: 1499 ll. 2813-2818 ("mirai una fabrica marmorea tra gli arbori apparendo et sopra le tenelle cime il suo fastigio")
features.note: A building seen through a wood before it is reached: the book's standard way of introducing a monument, and a sightline the world does not currently have anywhere.

features.name: The perfuming vessel on harpies' feet, six flying spirits holding bowls of coals
features.note: "six naked shapes of flying spirites ... of two cubites high" in a ring, a candlestick-stem with the seventh bowl, little gold pots boiling rose-water, orange-flower, myrtle, laurel, elder. Fumes and a pulsing light.

features.name: The self-refilling fountain on four little wheels, with the pear diamond
features.note: "continually running with water, and reassuming the same" -- the hydraulics ("two small pypes on eyther sides, and running vp straight in the middest") are the kind of thing this book explains. A jet; the reassuming is not simulated.

features.name: The repository, a ship of gold on four wheels with fishes and water-monsters
features.note: Plate #32 is the great vessel "twice nymph height" (the tour lede mentions it); the repository here is a first reading and stands at the open east end.

features.name: Fourteen damsel musicians, seven a side of the jasper door
features.note: Mute: the site is silent by decision. They stand; their instruments change with every service in the book and do not here.

features.name: The three that wait on the Queen: carver, plate, towel
features.note: and "one of those three which in the last chaunge attended ... did represent in her behauiour the sweet iesture and resemblance of Polia" (p. 156), who stands at the seventh table.

features.name: The vessel of coals the cloths are thrown into and come out clean
features.note: "the wonderfull straungest of all the rest." Asbestos cloth, which antiquity knew and Colonna treats as a marvel; the plaque keeps his wonder rather than explaining it away.

features.name: The chalice of gold with the coral tree on its cover, flowered with sapphire, jacinth and beryl
features.note: Carried by "the middlemost" of five nymphs in blue silk and gold; "monstrous great pearle" on the twig-tips.

features.name: The pierced gold balls stuffed with amber paste, given to every guest
features.note: "to the ende their hands, eyes, and sences should not be idle" -- a pomander. Ten lines; it belongs on the litter list for the court as much as on a table.

features.name: The perpetual fountain on an axle-tree with harpies at the angles (plate #32), "twice a nymph's height"
features.note:
Built and seen on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=366. The tour lede had promised it since the commentary was written and the world had never had it; the only trace was a line in a code comment above _buildBanquet naming the plate.

Built to Dallington pp. 158-159: an immoveable axle-tree with two wheels turning on it; an unequal quadrature three feet by two by six, which at the Roman foot of 0.296 m is 0.89 x 0.59 x 1.78; a harpy at every angle with wings stretched up to the breadth of the vessel above and tails turning into leaves over the void between them; the middle panel of each long side a triumph of satyrs and nymphs in half-relief; the ends bent in and rounded rather than squared, with the little sacrifice at its altar; and from the centre three vessels rising one out of the other, the second wider than the first, the third ridged and set with a row of coloured stones, a monster's head either side, a ring at the lip and a garland hung from it thickening toward the middle.

PLACED OUTSIDE THE COURT, and the reason is measured. Surface clearance across the whole court slab peaks at 0.40 m -- the banquet's seven tables, the throne, the chess pavement and the bath fill it. The first placement came off a probe that measured distance to object CENTRES rather than surfaces and put the fountain inside a wall at clearance 0.00. It now stands at (-24, 33) where there is 7.4 m, which suits the object: it is founded on an axle-tree with wheels, so it is furniture wheeled in with a course, and standing by the door waiting is what it is for.

Still imperfect, recorded rather than hidden: at (-24, 33) it is nearer the Water Labyrinth station at (-29.2, 34) than the court door, so it reads as the labyrinth's furniture rather than the banquet's. Cost: +13 meshes, +3 796 triangles.

features.name: Trumpets and cornets at every change, and the singers "that would haue caused the Syrens to sleepe"
features.note: The site is silent by standing decision.

research.note: Enumerated from the arbour and three-doors passages while building the jasmine arbour and cataloguing Poliphilo’s utterances. Not a full chapter pass. Dimensional and topographical pass of 2026-09-08 (the scale research: DIMENSIONS.md, DIRECTIONS.md, WOODS.md). This pass read the chapter for measurements, orientation and ground, not for its whole inventory.

features.name: The arbour of sweet jessamine, where he first sees Polia
features.note: Rebuilt 2026-09-07 as the tunnel the book describes -- "lifting vppe and bending ouer ... and entring in vnder the same" -- replacing four columns under a flat slab. The "flowers of three sortes commixt" are Rhizopoulou 2016’s three jasmines, red, yellow and white. One of only two things the Venice edition illustrates twice.

features.name: The three doors, and his choice of the third
features.note: His recoil from Philtronia’s house of Voluptuousness, immediately after choosing it, is now in the Poliphilo layer (our p. 197).

features.name: The doubt: is this nymph Polia?
features.note: The book’s central crisis and its best-recorded speech (five utterances in the Poliphilo layer). The world stages the meeting but not the doubt.

features.name: The three doors hewn in the living rock
features.built_as: world/portal.js _buildDoorsWall; the meadow exclusion in world/nature.js
features.note:
Built and verified on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=361, standing at the station (0, 21) looking north to the gates at z = 12.

The note this replaces described a build that no longer exists: "a free-standing 29 m masonry wall on a garden axis, the wrong ground, the wrong material and the wrong mood". The wall with its entablature and Corinthian columns — the opposite of "as plaine as might be" — had already been replaced by rock: a bank of boulders rising behind and above the gates, a straight-cut rock face with the three openings hewn from it, rough reveals, and the green moss the book gives the right-hand gate's leaves. So the material and the mood were right and the ledger had simply not been told.

What was still wrong was the GROUND, which is the third of the three faults and the one the book is most insistent about: "without any greene grasse or hearbe". The meadow was excluded from a strip only 2.8 m deep at the foot of the rock, so grass grew over the whole approach a reader actually crosses, and the stony ground stopped short of it. Now the exclusion covers the seat (x -15.5..15.5, z 5.5..19.5), the stone apron runs back to z = 19 to meet it, and 54 broken stones are strewn across it for "full of broken and nybled stones" — small, flat and un-collided, since the book's complaint is that the place is harsh underfoot, not that it is hard to cross.

Cost, measured: 5 621 -> 5 625 meshes and 3 101 652 -> 3 103 586 triangles. The 54 stones merge to about four draws because they share a material.

Still short of the book in one respect, recorded rather than hidden: the crags rise "as high as a man might looke to" and ours are a bank of boulders a few metres tall. The mountains behind are not built.

features.name: Polia's garden: a hundred ivied arches round it
features.note: An arcade 5 paces high and 3 across, "and there were a hundred Arches to the compassing of this garden" — 444 m of circumference, so 141 m across, with an altar of a cube, a red jasper disc and a black triangle at its centre. The station has a radius of 7. The clearest single measure of the compression the 2026-09-08 pass found.

research.note: Read end to end, pp. 284-289, with the boat's description from XIX pp. 276-277 and XXI p. 290. Six pages, no plate, and a station ("The Shore to Cythera") whose tour note already described the prow-for-stern boat and the cyan standard with three hieroglyphs -- while the world had a generic skiff with a sail. The crossing itself is a teleport (digit 0), not a voyage.

features.name: Cupid's exeres -- the six-oared boat, prow for poop
features.source: ours p. 276 (hull, balm, sandalwood and aloewood, gold nails with gems, red thwarts); p. 284 ("for its poop the prow"); p. 290
features.note: Both ends alike. No sail: p. 290 has Cupid "making sail with his spread wings".

features.name: Six ivory oars in gold rowlocks
features.note: "of illustrious and snowy ivory ... the rowlocks of gold, and the oar-thongs of commixed and twisted silk"

features.name: The six rowing nymphs, named: Aselgia, Neolea, Chlidonia, Olvolia, Adea, Cypria
features.source: ours p. 277 (names and dress), p. 285 (their six-voice song)
features.note: Three pairs: cloth-of-gold on cyan, Babylonian sea-purple, slashed melledarum with gold foil. Blond and raven by turns. Labelled with what their names mean.

features.name: The golden spear and the cyan-silk standard: vase with flame, the world, an osier withy
features.note: The three signs are on the silk, in gold thread and pearl, both faces alike; the reading AMOR VINCIT OMNIA is on a plaque by the pier, because reading it is Poliphilo's act, not the cloth's. The silk flutters "at the soft breaths of the spring-bearing zephyr".

features.name: Cupid at the prow, wings "of various and most-pleasant colouring" as the sail
features.note: Rainbow-banded feathered wings, spread. His multiform aspect ("twin ... triple ... infinite effigies", p. 285) is not attempted.

features.name: The six-voice chromatic song at the oars, and Polia's answer in the Lydian mode
features.note: The site is silent by standing decision (DECISIONS 2026-09-04). The tour note carries it.

features.name: The voyage itself: the boat "like a light water-skater" over the calm sea
features.note: Digit 0 is a teleport to the island. A ridden crossing -- the walker seated in the poop, the boat under way, the nymphs at the oars, arriving at the landing -- is the obvious thing and a real piece of work: the boat would have to be a mover like the triumph floats, and the island group is culled by distance.

features.name: The sea-gods' homage to Cupid at the departure
features.note: Belongs to XIX's ledger by page but to the shore by place. Neptune, tritons and nereids "submerging themselves, and thence bursting up" (p. 281). Not built.

research.note: Read end to end, pp. 369-379. The LAST chapter of Book I, eleven pages, and it carries NO WOODCUT — which is exactly why it went unbuilt: every coverage check this project ran before the ledger was driven by the plate catalogue, and the tour stop "The Tomb of Adonis" had been pointing at cythera_theatre's geometry since the commentary was written. The same shape as chapter V and the vaults. ROUTER.md rule 6.

features.name: The sacred fountain of Adonis, a hexagon of twelve paces
features.note: "shaped as a hexagon and twelve paces in its surrounding measure"; banks "hedged about and adorned with borders of Macedonian marble, not red, but of itself lustrous and veined" (p. 370).

features.name: The golden serpent from the cleft of rock
features.note: "cast in a globed coil, to curb the force of the water — which, by a free and straight pipe, would have scattered beyond the limits of the fountain": the book gives the hydraulics as design criticism, so the coil is built as three falling rings and the jet is short.

features.name: The cloister of orange, lemon and citron, "in an alternating marriage"
features.note: four paces off the marble border; "full of every singing bird — chiefly of nightingales, of thrushes, and of solitary blackbirds", which are built as perching birds.

features.name: The foot-high lattice of red sandalwood, and the WHITE hundred-petalled roses
features.source: ours p. 371, with the rite at pp. 375-376
features.note: The roses are white and that is the point of the whole station: they are not dyed purple until the liquor is drawn from the repository at the Ides, and Poliphilo sees them before the rite — "all the whitest roses, AS AT PRESENT THEY APPEAR, are re-dyed in purple colour".

features.name: The grove of cornel-cherry, cypress, palm, poplar and pine
features.note: trunks "clear of a single obstructing branch, [so] the free air of the neighbouring parts could be beautifully seen through". Cornel stands as plum and poplar as willow: the two species the SPECIES table does not carry.

features.name: The tessellated pavement grassed with sheared thyme
features.note: "all tressed with tiniest fragrant thyme … with an even shearing".

features.name: The emissary rivulet under the manna-ashes
features.note: "a most pleasing little rivulet carried off the liquid flowing waters … beneath the leaf-bearing manna-ashes with a soft and gentle murmur". It is also the drain the stripped roses are thrown into at the Ides.

features.name: The alabaster sepulchre of Adonis, five feet long
features.note: socle, chest and cornice; the two carved long sides drawn as reliefs (see _adonisRelief).

features.name: The two carved sides: Venus torn in the roses, and Adonis and the boar
features.note: One side: Venus coming naked from the fountain, tearing her divine calf in the rose-bushes, and Cupid gathering the purple blood into an oyster-shell. The other: Adonis among shepherd-hunters, dogs and the dead boar, and Venus falling "into the pitiful embraces of three half-swooning nymphs".

features.name: The jacinth stopping the repository, burning unsteadily
features.note: "of a transparent vermilion colour, with great coruscation of flaming splendour, burning unsteadily by the light set opposite" — so it is lit from behind, by a point light on the pulse list.

features.name: Venus in three-coloured sardonyx, in childbed, giving suck to Cupid
features.note: The stone is the conceit: the body cut from the milky vein of the onyx and the drapery from the red. Built recumbent, as a tomb effigy, and deliberately NOT as a painted cut-out — the book has stone here, not a painting. Her foot lies out over the rim for the nymphs to kneel and kiss, with the distich beneath it.

features.name: NON LAC SAEVE PVER, LACHRYMAS SED SVGIS AMARAS
features.note: the whole distich, with a plain English rendering under it.

features.name: The yearly rite of the Kalends of May, and the re-dyeing of the roses
features.note: Named on a plaque at the station, but not enacted. It is a four-part ceremony with a calendar — stripping and heaping on the eve of the Kalends, the overnight reflowering to the same number, the scattering into the fountain and the rivulet on the Ides, the unsealing of the repository, the oyster-shell of divine gore, the purpling of the roses, and three lustrations. It wants the same treatment as the Triumphs: a timed sequence you can stand in.
